note: Known answers for the embedding space. scripts/v2/embed_canary.py embeds these texts and refuses to let anything write vectors unless every one comes back byte-identical. The texts are original, written for this file, so nothing here is licensed prose. Editing a text or adding a case means bumping canarySet; regenerating the vectors is only legitimate when the space is MEANT to move (a VECTOR_EPOCH bump, a model change, a settings change with a full re-embed in the same pass) - never to get a failing run going, because dataset.meta.json publishes spaceId as the name of the space the corpus is in.
vectorEncoding: base64 of the int8 row, one byte per dimension, two's complement

cases.why: The lean document shape the corpus is actually built in (ComposedDoc.buildLean): fact clauses, a Themes clause, a Plot clause. A probe that never looks like the real input would let a change that only bites on that shape through.
cases.text: Directed by Ana Ruiz-Vidal. Genres: Drama, Mystery. Themes: coastal town, missing person, grief, unreliable memory, slow burn, bureaucratic horror. Plot: A municipal auditor is sent to reconcile forty years of harbour accounts in a fishing settlement that has been quietly writing down a larger version of itself since the cannery first threatened to close. The fiction turns out to be load-bearing: the ferry timetable, the school grant and the cannery insurance all rest on berths that were never built. Every correction he drafts would take a real roof off a real family.

cases.why: Long enough to run most of the way to the 1024-token cap without reaching it, so it exercises a long sequence while staying on the near side of truncation. Short texts survive differences that a long one does not.
cases.text: In the winter of 1974 a municipal auditor named Tomasz Weir is sent to a fishing settlement on the northern coast to reconcile forty years of harbour accounts that nobody has ever questioned. The settlement has one road, one chapel, one cannery, and a lighthouse that was automated a decade earlier but is still staffed on paper by a keeper who draws a salary and files a monthly ledger in a careful looping hand. Weir arrives expecting a week of arithmetic. He finds instead that the ledgers describe a harbour that does not exist: berths numbered past the length of the quay, tonnages that would have sunk the boats said to have carried them, and a standing line for lamp oil in a tower that has run on mains electricity since before the keeper was born. The keeper, an unhurried woman named Halla Brekke, does not deny any of it. She explains that the settlement has been writing down a slightly larger version of itself since the year the cannery first threatened to close, and that the extra berths and the phantom tonnage were how the harbour kept its subsidy, its ferry, and eventually its school. The arithmetic was never meant to deceive an auditor. It was meant to describe a town the people there intended to become, and it was maintained with the same seriousness as the tide tables. Weir begins the work of unwinding it and discovers that the fiction has grown load-bearing. The ferry timetable is calculated from the invented tonnage. The chapel roof was repaired with a grant awarded against a population that includes nineteen people who were counted twice. The cannery insurance rests on a cold store that was built, burned down in 1961, and never removed from the record, so that every subsequent claim has been settled against a building that no longer stands. Each thread he pulls is attached to something a living person depends on, and each correction he drafts would, if filed, take a real roof off a real family. The middle hour is the ordinary texture of an audit: photocopies, weighing scales, a borrowed bicycle, long silences in a guesthouse dining room where the other residents stop talking when he sits down. Weir is never threatened and never romanced. He is simply and continuously fed, housed, driven to the quay in bad weather, and shown the school. The pressure on him is made entirely of hospitality, and the film is careful to let the audience feel how much harder that is to refuse than a bribe. The turn comes when Weir finds his own predecessor in the files. Twelve years earlier another auditor made the same discovery, wrote the same report, and then submitted a second, shorter document certifying the accounts as sound. Both are in the box, filed consecutively, in the same hand. Nobody hid the first one. It was simply never sent, and the town kept it the way it keeps everything. Weir finishes his report on the last night of the storm season and reads it aloud to Brekke in the lamp room, where the automated light turns above them on its own schedule and neither of them has anything to do with it. She listens to the whole thing without interrupting. Then she asks him what he intends the town to be, given that his numbers describe one town and hers describe another, and only one of the two has a school in it. The final scene is the ferry leaving in grey light. Weir is aboard with a briefcase. The film does not show which report is inside it, and cuts as the lighthouse passes out of frame.

cases.why: Comfortably past 1024 tokens, so the answer depends on where the service truncates. It pins MAX_TOKENS the way the other cases cannot: at a different cap this vector changes and nothing else about the service has to.
cases.text: Fifty years after the last commercial flight, a salvage cooperative working the drowned approach roads of a coastal airport recovers an intact flight recorder from an aircraft that was never reported missing. The recorder is not from a crash. Its final entry is a routine landing checklist, completed and read back, followed by nine hours of cabin silence and then the sound of someone opening the cockpit door from the outside. Idris Nabera, the cooperative archivist, is the only member with the clearance and the patience to transcribe it. She works from a barge moored above the old terminal, in a workshop built into a baggage hall, and the film treats her equipment with documentary attention: the drying racks for salt-damaged tape, the improvised spool cut from a bicycle wheel, the long electrolysis baths that take a fortnight to render a corroded contact readable. Her transcription advances four seconds at a time. The registration on the recorder belongs to an aircraft that, according to every surviving register, was scrapped eleven years before the flight it recorded. Idris assumes a clerical error, then a fraud, then something stranger: the maintenance logs she recovers alongside it are internally consistent, initialled by real engineers whose pension records she can still check, and describe two hundred and forty hours of service on an airframe that officially did not exist. Somebody kept a plane flying off the books for a year, staffed it, fuelled it, and filed nothing. The cooperative is not a research institution and cannot afford a mystery. Its charter pays by recovered mass, its barge is mortgaged to a salvage bank in the next estuary, and its members have been told twice that the approach roads will be closed to dredging when the seawall contract is let. Idris pursues the recorder anyway, in the hours the charter does not own, and the film is honest about what that costs the people who cover her shifts. Her closest ally is a diver named Rukmini Sahay who does not believe a word of the airframe story and helps her anyway, on the grounds that Idris has never once been wrong about a tape. The transcript, as it emerges, is mundane and then not. The crew are professionals. They run checklists, complain about a scheduling office, discuss a colleague in hospital, and describe the weather at an airfield that closed to civil traffic in the year they are supposedly flying. Their callsign is answered. The voice answering them uses a phraseology that went out of use a generation before the recording and gives them a runway that was resurfaced into a solar farm. None of it is spoken as if it were strange. The crew are not lost and the controller is not confused; both sides are working, competently, inside a version of the coast that no longer exists on any chart Idris can find. She stops looking for a hoax at the point where the transcript includes a wind check that matches, to the knot and the degree, an entry in a handwritten weather log she recovered from a different wreck two years earlier and has never published. The film declines to explain this. Its interest is in what a person does with an answer that cannot be filed. Idris is an archivist by training and by temperament, and the third act is the slow discovery that her profession has no category for the thing she is holding. The regional archive will not accession a recording from an aircraft with no legal existence. The salvage bank wants the mass. A journalist offers to make her briefly famous and is plainly going to make her briefly ridiculous. Rukmini wants her to put it in a box and go back to work, and says so kindly, and is probably right. What Idris does instead is finish it. She spends the last of the season rendering the final nine hours, the silence, in full, at the cost of the contract the cooperative needed, and in doing so establishes that the silence is not empty. There is a cabin tone, a pressurisation cycle, and at intervals the small percussive sounds of a person moving unhurriedly through a galley. Somebody was aboard for those nine hours and did not speak, and the recorder ran out before they landed or did not land. The last sequence is the handover. Idris crates the recorder, the transcript, the weather log and her own working notes, and takes them not to the regional archive but to a school on the landward side of the seawall, where a teacher she has never met accepts the crate because a child in her class asked a question about the airport and she did not have an answer. The film ends on the crate being carried up a staircase, and on a corridor window through which the drowned terminal is visible at low tide, and gives no account of what is in the last nine hours or who was walking through the galley. What it has established instead is a chain of custody: a thing that could not be filed has been kept anyway, by someone who will keep it, which is the only ending an archivist story is entitled to.
